# Occasion and audience

## What this deck is made for

- Occasion: a training at the start of the build, or a refresher before an
  audit
- Audience: `practitioners`
- Length: 60 minutes, with questions in between
- What the listeners already know: the terms risk, control, scope and the three
  objectives

::: {.notes}
This slide is not presented. The deck for the leadership sits beside it and is
a different talk: it ends at four decisions, this one ends at an order of work.
Neither is the shortened version of the other.
:::

# What it is about

## The subject in one sentence

ISO/IEC 27001 says what an organisation has to be able to show for its
information security to be steered and not merely done, and clauses 4 to 10 are
the order in which that gets built.

## Why it concerns the practitioners

- Those clauses are the list an audit asks against
- Every clause gives the same question: is this here, and where is it written
  down
- Anyone who knows the order saves themselves the work done twice

# The seven clauses

## Clause 4: the context

- What surrounds the organisation and who expects something of it
- The scope gets cut out of that, and the interfaces outward belong expressly
  inside
- Result: a written determination, not a slide
- ISO/IEC 27001:2022, 4.1, 4.2, 4.3

## Clause 5: the leadership

- Policy, responsibilities, and what the leadership has to do itself
- These clauses cannot be replaced by diligence in clause 8
- ISO/IEC 27001:2022, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3

## Clause 6: the planning

- The heart sits here: assess risks, treat them, and determine the controls
  only out of the treatment
- The comparison against the annex comes after and looks for what was forgotten
- The statement of applicability is the result, not the form
- ISO/IEC 27001:2022, 6.1.2, 6.1.3, 6.2

## Clause 7: the resources

- People, competence, awareness, communication
- And the documented information: almost every requirement ends in a record
- ISO/IEC 27001:2022, 7.1 to 7.5

## Clause 8: the doing

- Assessment and treatment, now actually carried out and recorded
- The commonest finding is not a missing procedure but one that has not run
  since it was introduced
- ISO/IEC 27001:2022, 8.2, 8.3

## Clause 9: the checking

- Monitoring, measuring, analysing and evaluating are four different
  activities
- With the internal audit and the management review beside them
- ISO/IEC 27001:2022, 9.1, 9.2, 9.3

## Clause 10: the improving

- Continual improvement, including when nothing is broken
- And the corrective action, which removes the cause and not the single case
- ISO/IEC 27001:2022, 10.1, 10.2

# The order it all hangs on

## Why the annex does not come first

- The controls follow from the treatment of the risks, and the comparison
  against the annex comes after that
- The other way round produces an inventory that looks like a management system
  and carries no reasoning
- It shows up only in the statement of applicability, where every number lacks
  a why
- ISO/IEC 27001:2022, 6.1.3

## How to recognise the order turned around

- The statement of applicability was finished before the risk register
- No line in it points back at a risk
- Every residual risk stands at zero

# What to do or decide afterwards

## The next steps

- Read the scope and establish whether it is written down
- Take one first risk all the way through to the line in the statement of
  applicability, checking the order while doing it
- For every clause from 4 to 10, note where the record sits or that there is
  none
- Who, by when: belongs in the discussion and not on this slide
